claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lee et al., 2015; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Yizhar et al., 2011).

claims.claim: A better understanding of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter systems during developmental learning may be of therapeutic relevance.
claims.source: Excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter systems are involved in severe mental disorders (Lee et al., 2015; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Yizhar et al., 2011), which is why a better understanding of these systems during developmental learning may be of therapeutic relevance.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the involvement of these systems in mental disorders.

claims.claim: Normal development of birdsong requires early sensory experience, similar to human speech development.
claims.source: Similar to human speech development (Neville and Bavelier, 2002), the normal development of birdsong requires early sensory experience (Barrington, 1773; Beecher and Brenowitz, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Barrington, 1773; Beecher and Brenowitz, 2005; Neville and Bavelier, 2002).

claims.claim: Adult birdsong is generated and temporally controlled by interactions among inhibitory and excitatory neurons in HVC.
claims.source: Adult birdsong is generated and temporally controlled by interactions among inhibitory and excitatory neurons in HVC (Aronov et al., 2008; Kosche et al., 2015; Long and Fee, 2008; Mooney and Prather, 2005; Nottebohm et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Aronov et al., 2008; Kosche et al., 2015; Long and Fee, 2008; Mooney and Prather, 2005; Nottebohm et al., 1976).

claims.claim: Blockage of NMDA-mediated synaptic transmission in HVC during tutor exposure abolishes normal song development.
claims.source: An important role of excitation is to participate in successful acquisition of a template of tutor song, because blockage of NMDA-mediated (excitatory) synaptic transmission in HVC during tutor exposure abolishes normal song development (Roberts et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Roberts et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The strength of HVC inhibition correlates with the learned portions of song but not with age.
claims.source: One important role of HVC inhibition may be to protect HVC neurons after tutoring from further sensory influence, as the strength of HVC inhibition correlates with the learned portions of song but not with age (Vallentin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Vallentin et al., 2016).

claims.claim: One day of tutor exposure led to a 26 ± 5% decrease in HVC asymmetric (excitatory) synapse density.
claims.source: We found that one day of tutor exposure led to a 26 ± 5% decrease in the HVC asymmetric (excitatory) synapse density (p = 3*10−9, linear mixed effect (LME) model with bird group as fixed effect and bird identity as random effect, df = 1152, n = 4 SHORT birds and n = 4 ISO birds, see Materials and methods), Figure 1B,C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 3*10−9), and is shown in Figure 1B,C.

claims.claim: HVC symmetric (inhibitory) synapse density increased by about 20 ± 10% during one day of tutor exposure.
claims.source: In contrast, the HVC symmetric (inhibitory) synapse density increased by about 20 ± 10% during one day of tutor exposure (p = 0.05, LME model, df = 1152, n=4 SHORT and n=4 ISO birds), Figure 1B,D.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.05), and is shown in Figure 1B,D.

claims.claim: Upon first tutoring and within 24 hr, the percent inhibitory synapses in HVC rose by 42% from on average 19% (ISO group) to 27% (SHORT group).
claims.source: In combination, upon first tutoring and within 24 hr, the percent inhibitory synapses in HVC rose by 42% from on average 19% (ISO group) to 27% (SHORT group, p = 1.7*10−6, LME model with 32 observations, two fixed effect coefficients, and eight random effect coefficients, see Materials and methods), Figure 1E.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 1.7*10−6), and is shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: 24 days of tutoring led to a decrease in excitatory synapse density of 37 ± 1% compared with the ISO group.
claims.source: Compared with the ISO group, we found that 24 days of tutoring led to a decrease in excitatory synapse density of 37 ± 1% (p = 4.5*10−18, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds) and to a decrease in inhibitory synapse density of 30 ± 2% (p = 0.003, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 4.5*10−18).

claims.claim: 24 days of tutoring led to a decrease in inhibitory synapse density of 30 ± 2% compared with the ISO group.
claims.source: Compared with the ISO group, we found that 24 days of tutoring led to a decrease in excitatory synapse density of 37 ± 1% (p = 4.5*10−18, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds) and to a decrease in inhibitory synapse density of 30 ± 2% (p = 0.003, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.003).

claims.claim: The percent inhibitory synapses in LONG birds was barely larger than in ISO birds (21% vs 20%).
claims.source: Altogether, tutoring induced a synaptic bias towards inhibition that was transient, because the percent inhibitory synapses in LONG birds was barely larger than in ISO birds (21% vs 20%, p = 0.48, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.48).

claims.claim: Tutoring induced a synaptic bias towards inhibition that was transient.
claims.source: Altogether, tutoring induced a synaptic bias towards inhibition that was transient, because the percent inhibitory synapses in LONG birds was barely larger than in ISO birds (21% vs 20%, p = 0.48, LME model, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 ISO birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing that the initial increase in inhibitory synapses (SHORT group) returned to near-baseline levels after extended tutoring (LONG group).

claims.claim: LONG60 birds tutored in 24 sessions of 90 min produced more accurate song copies than LONG birds, with their average similarity score exceeding that of LONG birds by 21% on average.
claims.source: As expected, LONG60 birds tutored in 24 sessions of 90 min produced more accurate song copies: their average similarity score with tutor song exceeded that of LONG birds by 21% on average (p = 0.006, nonzero fixed effect of 0.21 in LME model comparing n = 4 LONG60 with n = 4 LONG birds, t = 2.41, df = 158), Figure 2B.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from song analysis and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.006), and is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: At 60 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities were lower in tutored than in untutored birds.
claims.source: Extended tutoring was again observed together with synapse removal: at 60 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities were lower in tutored than in untutored birds (p = 10−30 for excitatory density and p = 3*10−6 for inhibitory density, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 ISO60 birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 10−30 for excitatory and p = 3*10−6 for inhibitory).

claims.claim: At 90 dph, synapse densities remained lower in tutored birds compared to their age-matched untutored controls.
claims.source: At 90 dph, densities remained lower in tutored birds compared to their age-matched untutored controls (p = 0.02 for excitatory density and p = 3*10−5 for inhibitory density, LME model, n = 4 LONG90 and n = 4 ISO90 birds), Figure 2C,D.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.02 for excitatory and p = 3*10−5 for inhibitory), and is shown in Figure 2C,D.

claims.claim: Sparse tutoring was associated with lower excitatory synapse densities than dense tutoring.
claims.source: Sparse tutoring was associated with lower excitatory synapse densities than dense tutoring (p = 3*10−6, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG birds), suggesting that pruning of excitatory synapses is related to song maturation (i.e., increases in song similarity scores).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 3*10−6).

claims.claim: Pruning of excitatory synapses is related to song maturation (i.e., increases in song similarity scores).
claims.source: Sparse tutoring was associated with lower excitatory synapse densities than dense tutoring (p = 3*10−6, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG birds), suggesting that pruning of excitatory synapses is related to song maturation (i.e., increases in song similarity scores).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that sparse tutoring (which produces better song copies) is associated with lower excitatory synapse densities.

claims.claim: There was a negative correlation between song similarity scores and excitatory synapse densities (r = −0.77, p = 0.026).
claims.source: Indeed, there was a negative correlation between song similarity scores and excitatory synapse densities (r = −0.77, p = 0.026, Pearson correlation coefficient, n = 4 LONG and n = 4 LONG60 birds), Figure 2E.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from correlation analysis (Pearson correlation, r = −0.77, p = 0.026), and is shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Sparse tutoring did not appear to alter inhibitory synapse densities at 60 dph.
claims.source: Sparse tutoring did not appear to alter inhibitory synapse densities at 60 dph (p = 0.2, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.2).

claims.claim: In tutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, excitatory synapse densities increased.
claims.source: In tutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, excitatory synapse densities increased (p = 9*10−6, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG90 birds) whereas inhibitory synapse densities decreased (p = 0.03, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG90 birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 9*10−6).

claims.claim: In tutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, inhibitory synapse densities decreased.
claims.source: In tutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, excitatory synapse densities increased (p = 9*10−6, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG90 birds) whereas inhibitory synapse densities decreased (p = 0.03, LME model, n = 4 LONG60 and n = 4 LONG90 birds).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.03).

claims.claim: Over the course of song development, the percentage of inhibitory synapses in tutored birds ranged from 7% at the onset of song development (30 dph), to roughly 23% at 60 dph, down to 14% at 90 dph.
claims.source: As a consequence, over the course of song development, the percentage of inhibitory synapses in tutored birds ranged from 7% at the onset of song development (30 dph), to roughly 23% at 60 dph, down to 14% at 90 dph.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements across different developmental time points.

claims.claim: The developmental trajectory of the synaptic balance is highly dynamic in normally tutored birds.
claims.source: Thus, the developmental trajectory of the synaptic balance is highly dynamic in normally tutored birds.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed changes in the percentage of inhibitory synapses across development.

claims.claim: The age-related peak-decline trend of inhibitory synapse densities occurred irrespective of sensory experience (it was seen in both tutored and untutored birds).
claims.source: The age-related peak-decline trend of inhibitory synapse densities occurred irrespective of sensory experience (it was seen in both tutored and untutored birds, Figure 2D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements in both tutored and untutored birds, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In untutored birds, excitatory synapse densities did not decrease until past closure of the critical period.
claims.source: By contrast, in untutored birds, excitatory synapse densities did not decrease until past closure of the critical period, Figure 2C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements in untutored birds, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Abundance of HVC excitatory synapses in young birds is not a requirement for song production, but instead signals readiness for sensory memory formation.
claims.source: These observations suggest that abundance of HVC excitatory synapses in young birds is not a requirement for song production, but that instead it signals readiness for sensory memory formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that young birds at 30 dph have high excitatory synapse densities but do not yet sing, except for occasional unstructured subsongs that do not require HVC.

claims.claim: In untutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities decreased.
claims.source: Moreover, in untutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities decreased (p = 0.009 for excitatory and p = 3*10−6 for inhibitory synapses, LME model, n = 4 ISO60 and n = 4 ISO90 birds), suggesting that high synapse densities are costly and therefore not maintained beyond the critical period.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (LME model, p = 0.009 for excitatory and p = 3*10−6 for inhibitory).

claims.claim: High synapse densities are costly and therefore not maintained beyond the critical period.
claims.source: Moreover, in untutored birds from 60 to 90 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities decreased (p = 0.009 for excitatory and p = 3*10−6 for inhibitory synapses, LME model, n = 4 ISO60 and n = 4 ISO90 birds), suggesting that high synapse densities are costly and therefore not maintained beyond the critical period.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that synapse densities decrease in untutored birds after the critical period.

claims.claim: One day of tutoring was associated with a 22% increase in inhibitory synapse densities.
claims.source: Combining the ISO and ISO60 birds, we found that one day of tutoring was associated with a 22% increase in inhibitory synapse densities (p = 0.016, n = 8 ISO and n = 4 SHORT birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test) and with a 33% decrease in excitatory synapse density (p = 0.008, n = 8 ISO and n = 4 SHORT birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (Wilcoxon ranksum test, p = 0.016).

claims.claim: One day of tutoring was associated with a 33% decrease in excitatory synapse density.
claims.source: Combining the ISO and ISO60 birds, we found that one day of tutoring was associated with a 22% increase in inhibitory synapse densities (p = 0.016, n = 8 ISO and n = 4 SHORT birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test) and with a 33% decrease in excitatory synapse density (p = 0.008, n = 8 ISO and n = 4 SHORT birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (Wilcoxon ranksum test, p = 0.008).

claims.claim: One day of tutoring was associated with an increase in the percentage of inhibitory synapses from 20% to 29%.
claims.source: In combination, one day of tutoring was associated with an increase in the percentage of inhibitory synapses from 20% to 29% (p = 0.004, n = 4 SHORT and n = 8 ISO birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (Wilcoxon ranksum test, p = 0.004).

claims.claim: Extended tutoring was associated with a decrease in inhibitory and excitatory synapse densities of 38% and 50%, respectively.
claims.source: Combining also the LONG and LONG60 birds, we found that extended tutoring was associated with a decrease in inhibitory and excitatory synapse densities of 38% and 50%, respectively (both tests p = 0.00016, n = 8 LONG and n = 8 ISO birds, Wilcoxon ranksum test), Figure 3A,B.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis (Wilcoxon ranksum test, p = 0.00016), and is shown in Figure 3A,B.

claims.claim: Tutoring has no major influence on HVC size.
claims.source: Tutoring has no major influence on HVC size (Bottjer et al., 1985; Herrmann and Bischof, 1986; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1988).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bottjer et al., 1985; Herrmann and Bischof, 1986; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1988).

claims.claim: HVC volumes were variable across animals but did not strongly depend on age or treatment, with the exception that the average HVC volume in 30 dph-old birds was about 30% smaller than in the other bird groups.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that HVC volumes were variable across animals but did not strongly depend on age or treatment, with the exception that the average HVC volume in 30 dph-old birds was about 30% smaller than in the other bird groups (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from HVC volume measurements, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LONG60 birds tended to have fewer excitatory HVC synapses than did ISO30 birds, evidencing in sparse tutored birds from early to mid-development a process of net excitatory synapse elimination.
claims.source: Despite this moderate growth in HVC volume from 30 to 60 dph, LONG60 birds tended to have fewer excitatory HVC synapses than did ISO30 birds, evidencing in sparse tutored birds from early to mid-development a process of net excitatory synapse elimination.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of excitatory synapse numbers between LONG60 and ISO30 birds, despite HVC volume growth.

claims.claim: Synapse sizes (their physical volumes) were well approximated by log-normal distributions.
claims.source: We found that synapse sizes (their physical volumes) were well approximated by log-normal distributions, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synapse size measurements and statistical fitting, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Excitatory synapses in SHORT birds were 40% larger than in ISO birds.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we found an effect of 40% larger excitatory synapses in SHORT birds compared to ISO birds (LME, p = 0.05), Figure 4D.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synapse size measurements and statistical analysis (LME, p = 0.05), and is shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Extended tutoring was not associated with significant size changes of excitatory synapses.
claims.source: Extended tutoring was not associated with significant size changes of excitatory synapses (LME, ISO vs LONG, p = 0.42).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synapse size measurements and statistical analysis (LME, p = 0.42).

claims.claim: Sizes of inhibitory synapses were not affected by either short or long tutoring.
claims.source: Sizes of inhibitory synapses were not affected by either short or long tutoring (LME, p > 0.05), Figure 4E.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synapse size measurements and statistical analysis (LME, p > 0.05), and is shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: There was no effect of tutoring on Feret diameters of either excitatory or inhibitory synapses.
claims.source: Also, we found no effect of tutoring on Feret diameters (directional measure of object size) of either excitatory or inhibitory synapses (LME, p > 0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Feret diameter measurements and statistical analysis (LME, p > 0.05).

claims.claim: Insertion and elimination of HVC synapses are age and experience dependent.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that insertion and elimination of HVC synapses are age and experience dependent.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing changes in synapse densities with age and tutoring experience.

claims.claim: There was a more than three-fold variation across age and experience in the relative density of inhibitory synapses.
claims.source: There was a strong decoupling among synapse types in that we observed a more than three-fold variation across age and experience in the relative density of inhibitory synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements showing variation in inhibitory synapse densities.

claims.claim: After extended tutor exposure, the density, ratio, and average sizes of synapses returned to levels close to those of age-matched untutored controls.
claims.source: After extended tutor exposure, the density, ratio, and average sizes of synapses returned to levels close to those of age-matched untutored controls, which hints at a structural homeostasis (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004) that is independent of learning experience.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements comparing LONG and ISO groups.

claims.claim: The return of synapse properties to baseline levels after extended tutoring hints at a structural homeostasis that is independent of learning experience.
claims.source: After extended tutor exposure, the density, ratio, and average sizes of synapses returned to levels close to those of age-matched untutored controls, which hints at a structural homeostasis (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004) that is independent of learning experience.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and draws on the concept of structural homeostasis from prior research (Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004).

claims.claim: Synapse density has been commonly observed to follow a peak-decline trend from youth to adulthood.
claims.source: Synapse density has been commonly observed to follow a peak-decline trend from youth to adulthood (Cragg, 1975; Herrmann and Arnold, 1991; Murphy and Magness, 1984; Winfield, 1981a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cragg, 1975; Herrmann and Arnold, 1991; Murphy and Magness, 1984; Winfield, 1981a).

claims.claim: The peak in synapse density is thought to represent overproduction of neuronal connections, reflecting elevated structural plasticity at the onset of behavioral development.
claims.source: The peak is thought to represent overproduction of neuronal connections, reflecting elevated structural plasticity at the onset of behavioral development.
claims.evidence: The claim draws on established scientific knowledge about synapse development.

claims.claim: In HVC of normally raised birds, there is an early peak-decline trend for excitatory synapses, and a late such trend in inhibitory synapses.
claims.source: In HVC of normally raised birds, we find an early peak-decline trend for excitatory synapses, and a late such trend in inhibitory synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements across developmental time points.

claims.claim: Excitatory synapses were formed very early and in untutored birds they were regulated at a constant rate throughout the sensory learning period from 30 to 60 dph.
claims.source: Excitatory synapses were formed very early and in untutored birds they were regulated at a constant rate throughout the sensory learning period from 30 to 60 dph.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements in untutored birds.

claims.claim: Inhibitory synapses were formed later, reminiscent of delayed development of inhibition in visual and auditory cortices.
claims.source: Inhibitory synapses were formed later, reminiscent of delayed development of inhibition in visual (Winfield, 1981b) and auditory cortices (Dorrn et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy measurements and citations to prior research (Winfield, 1981b; Dorrn et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Increases in inhibition tends to cause the end of experience-related plasticity.
claims.source: Given that increases in inhibition tends to cause the end of experience-related plasticity (Chen et al., 2011; Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000; Hensch, 2005; Iwai et al., 2003), the age- and tutoring dependent increases in inhibitory synapse densities we find raise the possibility that increased inhibition causes not only the closure of the sensory learning period but also accelerates the ending of structural plasticity right after tutoring.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Chen et al., 2011; Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000; Hensch, 2005; Iwai et al., 2003).

claims.claim: The age- and tutoring dependent increases in inhibitory synapse densities raise the possibility that increased inhibition causes not only the closure of the sensory learning period but also accelerates the ending of structural plasticity right after tutoring.
claims.source: Given that increases in inhibition tends to cause the end of experience-related plasticity (Chen et al., 2011; Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000; Hensch, 2005; Iwai et al., 2003), the age- and tutoring dependent increases in inhibitory synapse densities we find raise the possibility that increased inhibition causes not only the closure of the sensory learning period but also accelerates the ending of structural plasticity right after tutoring.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on inhibitory synapse densities and prior research on the role of inhibition in plasticity.

claims.claim: Processes of synapse formation and elimination are associated with sprouting and retraction of dendritic spines.
claims.source: Processes of synapse formation and elimination are associated with sprouting and retraction of dendritic spines (Holtmaat et al., 2006; Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Holtmaat et al., 2006; Trachtenberg et al., 2002).

claims.claim: Tutoring is associated with a rapid and monotonic decline in HVC spine turnover.
claims.source: Because tutoring is associated with a rapid and monotonic decline in HVC spine turnover (Roberts et al., 2010), there seems to be diminished requirement for structural plasticity right after tutoring, in line with our observed increase in inhibitory synapse density that supposedly closes critical period learning.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Roberts et al., 2010).

claims.claim: There seems to be diminished requirement for structural plasticity right after tutoring, in line with the observed increase in inhibitory synapse density that supposedly closes critical period learning.
claims.source: Because tutoring is associated with a rapid and monotonic decline in HVC spine turnover (Roberts et al., 2010), there seems to be diminished requirement for structural plasticity right after tutoring, in line with our observed increase in inhibitory synapse density that supposedly closes critical period learning.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed increase in inhibitory synapse density and prior research on spine turnover.

claims.claim: Synapse pruning tends to be an activity-dependent process, for example mediated by microglia.
claims.source: Synapse pruning tends to be an activity-dependent process, for example mediated by microglia (Schafer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schafer et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The better explanation for fewer excitatory synapses in sparsely tutored birds is their higher song maturity (better song imitation).
claims.source: Tutor exposure is associated with decreases in excitatory synapse densities, and so naively one would expect higher excitatory synapse densities in sparsely tutored birds compared to densely tutored birds. However, we find the opposite, and therefore the better explanation for fewer excitatory synapses in sparsely tutored birds is their higher song maturity (better song imitation).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that sparsely tutored birds have fewer excitatory synapses but better song imitation.

claims.claim: Excitatory connections have been proposed to implement a sequence-generating chain network.
claims.source: On the one hand, excitatory connections have been proposed to implement a sequence-generating chain network (Fee et al., 2004; Kornfeld et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fee et al., 2004; Kornfeld et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Elimination of HVC excitatory synapses during song maturation agrees with the sparse firing of excitatory motor-projecting neurons in adulthood.
claims.source: Elimination of HVC excitatory synapses during song maturation agrees with the sparse firing of excitatory motor-projecting neurons in adulthood (Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Hahnloser et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on synapse elimination and citations to prior research on neuronal firing patterns (Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Hahnloser et al., 2002).

claims.claim: Over the course of song maturation, HVC projection neurons fire first densely during each syllable and then sparsely during only a single syllable type.
claims.source: Over the course of song maturation, HVC projection neurons fire first densely during each syllable and then sparsely during only a single syllable type (Okubo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Okubo et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Sparsening of firing has been suggested to result from a synaptic chain splitting mechanism that underlies the transformation of immature subsongs into more stereotyped plastic songs.
claims.source: Such sparsening of firing has been suggested to result from a synaptic chain splitting mechanism that underlies the transformation of immature subsongs into more stereotyped plastic songs.
claims.evidence: The claim draws on established scientific knowledge about song development mechanisms.

claims.claim: The findings of progressive elimination of excitatory synapses up to 60 dph supports synaptic chain splitting.
claims.source: Our findings of progressive elimination of excitatory synapses up to 60 dph supports such chain splitting, whereas the subsequent insertion of excitatory synapses (LONG90 vs LONG60) could reflect a process of chain strengthening.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on excitatory synapse elimination.

claims.claim: The subsequent insertion of excitatory synapses (LONG90 vs LONG60) could reflect a process of chain strengthening.
claims.source: Our findings of progressive elimination of excitatory synapses up to 60 dph supports such chain splitting, whereas the subsequent insertion of excitatory synapses (LONG90 vs LONG60) could reflect a process of chain strengthening.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data on excitatory synapse insertion.

claims.claim: Excitatory synapses and their dendritic spines can be formed by repetitive motor training.
claims.source: On the other hand, excitatory synapses and their dendritic spines can be formed by repetitive motor training (Xu et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2012), which aligns with our observation of increasing excitatory synapse density towards adulthood.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Xu et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Optical ablation of task-specific spines in motor cortex can selectively disrupt newly acquired motor skills.
claims.source: Given that optical ablation of task-specific spines in motor cortex can selectively disrupt newly acquired motor skills (Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015), it is likely that the late-formed excitatory synapses between 60 and 90 dph contribute to increased motor performance in adults.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015).

claims.claim: It is likely that the late-formed excitatory synapses between 60 and 90 dph contribute to increased motor performance in adults.
claims.source: Given that optical ablation of task-specific spines in motor cortex can selectively disrupt newly acquired motor skills (Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015), it is likely that the late-formed excitatory synapses between 60 and 90 dph contribute to increased motor performance in adults.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on excitatory synapse insertion and prior research on motor skills.

claims.claim: The findings support the view that sensory memorization is associated with loss of excitatory synapses, whereas increases in motor performance are associated with insertion of excitatory synapses.
claims.source: Accordingly, our findings support the view that sensory memorization is associated with loss of excitatory synapses, whereas increases in motor performance are associated with insertion of excitatory synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on excitatory synapse dynamics across development.

claims.claim: There is a paradoxical finding of a net removal of inhibitory synapses (LONG vs ISO) during a developmental phase in which the strength of inhibition onto motor-projecting HVC neurons increases.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the biological context for studying synaptic reorganization during critical period learning in songbirds. These claims review prior work showing that brain structure during critical periods is regulated by age and sensory experience, that neuronal connections undergo experience-dependent modifications including synapse elimination, and that both excitatory and inhibitory transmissions shape sensory experience outcomes. The songbird model is justified by parallels to human speech development and prior findings on HVC's role in song generation and learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior research and establish the scientific rationale for the study. These background claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field and provide proper context for the experimental work that follows.

results.result: One day of tutor exposure causes rapid synaptic reorganization in HVC, with a 26-33% decrease in excitatory synapse density and a 20-22% increase in inhibitory synapse density. This results in the percentage of inhibitory synapses increasing from 19-20% to 27-29% within 24 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C34-C36 present consistent findings from two independent experiments with appropriate statistical analyses (LME models and Wilcoxon tests, all p<0.05). The sample sizes (n=4 per group) are modest but the effect sizes are large and statistically significant. The findings are internally consistent across both experiments.

results.result: Extended tutoring (24 days) leads to net removal of both excitatory (37-50% decrease) and inhibitory (30-38% decrease) synapses compared to untutored controls. The initial tutoring-induced bias toward inhibition is transient, as the percentage of inhibitory synapses returns to near-baseline levels (21% vs 20%) after extended tutoring.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 and C37 are well-supported by experimental data with strong statistical significance (p values ranging from 0.003 to 4.5×10⁻¹⁸). The finding that both synapse types decrease but return to similar proportions is internally consistent and demonstrates a dynamic homeostatic process. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-8 per group).

results.result: Sparse tutoring (90 min/day) produces better song copies than dense tutoring (24 hr/day), with 21% higher similarity scores. Sparse tutoring is associated with lower excitatory synapse densities, and there is a significant negative correlation (r=-0.77, p=0.026) between song similarity and excitatory synapse density, suggesting that excitatory synapse pruning is related to song maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C21-C23, and C61 present a coherent finding linking synaptic structure to behavioral outcome. The correlation analysis is appropriately conducted (Pearson correlation, n=8 birds total), though the sample size is modest. The interpretation that pruning relates to song maturation is reasonable given the data, though causality cannot be definitively established from correlation alone.

results.result: Developmental trajectory of synaptic balance in tutored birds is highly dynamic. At 60 dph, both excitatory and inhibitory synapse densities are lower in tutored than untutored birds. From 60 to 90 dph, excitatory densities increase while inhibitory densities decrease. The percentage of inhibitory synapses ranges from 7% at 30 dph, to 23% at 60 dph, down to 14% at 90 dph.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 and C25-C28 describe developmental changes with strong statistical support (p values from 0.03 to 10⁻³⁰). The dynamic trajectory is well-documented across multiple time points with appropriate controls. The findings reveal a complex, non-monotonic developmental pattern that is internally consistent.

results.result: Age-related changes in synapse densities differ between tutored and untutored birds. The peak-decline trend in inhibitory synapse density occurs regardless of tutoring experience. In untutored birds, excitatory synapse densities remain constant during the critical period (30-60 dph) but decrease afterward (60-90 dph), suggesting that high synapse densities are costly and not maintained beyond the critical period without learning experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C32-C33, and C53 demonstrate important differences between tutored and untutored developmental trajectories with appropriate statistical support (p values from 0.009 to 3×10⁻⁶). The interpretation about metabolic cost (C33) is reasonable inference from the data, though direct evidence of cost is not provided.

results.result: The abundance of excitatory synapses in young birds (30 dph) signals readiness for sensory memory formation rather than being required for song production. Despite HVC volume growth from 30 to 60 dph, sparsely tutored birds show net excitatory synapse elimination during this period.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C40 present reasonable inferences from the data. The interpretation is supported by the observation that young birds have high excitatory synapse densities but don't yet sing (except subsongs that don't require HVC), and by the comparison of synapse numbers across developmental stages accounting for volume changes.

results.result: Tutoring has no major influence on HVC size, with volumes being variable across animals but not strongly dependent on age or treatment, except that 30 dph birds have ~30% smaller HVC volumes than older birds.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by both citations to prior work and the authors' own measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. This finding is important for interpreting density measurements as reflecting actual synapse number changes rather than volume changes.

results.result: Synapse sizes follow log-normal distributions. One day of tutoring is associated with 40% larger excitatory synapses (p=0.05), but extended tutoring shows no significant size changes. Inhibitory synapse sizes and Feret diameters are not affected by tutoring.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by FIBSEM data and appropriate statistical analyses. The finding of transient excitatory synapse enlargement after short tutoring is interesting, though the p-value is marginal (p=0.05). The log-normal distribution fitting is well-validated with goodness-of-fit tests reported in the methods.

results.result: HVC synapse insertion and elimination are age- and experience-dependent, with more than three-fold variation in relative inhibitory synapse density across conditions. After extended tutoring, synaptic properties return to levels close to untutored controls, suggesting structural homeostasis independent of learning experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 synthesize the major findings appropriately. The homeostasis interpretation (C49) is reasonable given the data showing return to baseline after extended tutoring, though the mechanism remains speculative. The citation to Turrigiano and Nelson (2004) appropriately connects to established concepts.

results.result: The developmental pattern in HVC shows an early peak-decline trend for excitatory synapses and a late peak-decline trend for inhibitory synapses. Inhibitory synapses form later than excitatory synapses, reminiscent of delayed inhibition development in visual and auditory cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 and C54 appropriately contextualize the findings within established developmental neuroscience. The comparison to other sensory systems (C54) is supported by appropriate citations. The observed temporal offset between excitatory and inhibitory synapse development is clearly demonstrated in the data.

results.result: The age- and tutoring-dependent increases in inhibitory synapse density may cause both closure of the sensory learning period and accelerated ending of structural plasticity after tutoring. This interpretation is consistent with prior work showing that increased inhibition ends experience-related plasticity and that tutoring is associated with rapid decline in HVC spine turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 present a mechanistic interpretation well-supported by citations to prior research on inhibition and plasticity. The connection between the authors' structural findings and prior functional/behavioral work (Roberts et al., 2010) is logical and appropriately cautious in its claims.

results.result: The progressive elimination of excitatory synapses up to 60 dph supports a synaptic chain splitting mechanism underlying transformation of subsongs into stereotyped plastic songs. Subsequent insertion of excitatory synapses (60-90 dph) could reflect chain strengthening. This interpretation aligns with prior proposals that excitatory connections implement sequence-generating chain networks and with observations of sparse firing in adult HVC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are well-supported by appropriate citations and logical connection to the data. Claim C67 is appropriately marked as speculative. The interpretation connects structural findings to established models of HVC function, though direct evidence for chain splitting/strengthening mechanisms is not provided.

results.result: Late-formed excitatory synapses (60-90 dph) likely contribute to increased motor performance in adults, consistent with prior work showing that excitatory synapses can be formed by repetitive motor training and that task-specific spines are required for motor skills. The findings support the view that sensory memorization is associated with excitatory synapse loss, while motor performance increases are associated with excitatory synapse insertion.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 present a coherent interpretation connecting the developmental trajectory to distinct learning phases. The interpretation is supported by appropriate citations to motor learning literature. However, the distinction between sensory and motor phases is somewhat inferential, as direct measures of motor performance improvement are not provided.

results.result: The paradox of net inhibitory synapse removal during a phase when inhibitory strength increases can be reconciled by maturation processes such as AMPA receptor insertion at excitatory synapses (for which there is indirect evidence via increased synapse size) or by selective elimination of synapses that disinhibit local excitatory-inhibitory pools associated with learned syllables.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 acknowledge an apparent contradiction between structural and functional findings and propose plausible reconciliations. However, the evidence is indirect (synapse size as proxy for receptor content) and the disinhibition mechanism is largely speculative. The interpretation is reasonable but requires direct functional validation.

results.result: The removal of excitatory inputs aligns with developmental sharpening seen in auditory cortex. However, the relationship between structural preponderance of excitatory versus inhibitory synapses and functional excitatory-inhibitory balance remains unclear. Overall, the work provides a structural foundation for understanding developmental learning mechanisms and neurotransmitter system roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 appropriately acknowledge both the contributions and limitations of the work. The comparison to auditory cortex (C76) is supported by citation. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about structure-function relationships (C77) is scientifically appropriate. The summary claim (C78) is justified by the comprehensive dataset.

results.result: The findings have potential therapeutic relevance for mood disorders, which are linked to excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter imbalances. The alternating experience-dependent dynamics in inhibitory and excitatory synapses found in this study might help explain mixed reports of SSRI effects on cortical GABA and glutamate. Exposure therapies and pharmacological treatments might benefit from targeted manipulation of both excitation and inhibition considering their experience-dependent dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 extend the findings to clinical implications. While the basic science is sound, the therapeutic extrapolations are highly speculative. The connection between songbird synaptic dynamics and human psychiatric treatment (C84) is not directly supported by data. These claims represent reasonable discussion points but should not be considered established results.

results.result: The structural changes may be associated with holding a memory of tutor song. Memory could be held either by inhibitory synapses inserted after tutoring (supported by analogy to barrel cortex) or by irreversible removal of excitatory synapses representing notes/transitions not matched by tutor song. In this model, initially formed excitatory connections would represent the entire vocal repertoire space, with elimination representing non-tutor elements and strengthening representing tutor-matched elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 present speculative models of memory storage mechanisms. While the models are creative and consistent with the data, they lack direct experimental support. The analogy to barrel cortex (C87-C88) provides some support but is from a different system. These are reasonable hypotheses for future testing but should not be considered established results.

results.result: The main findings are that tutor exposure leads to excitatory synapse elimination in HVC, with better song imitation associated with fewer excitatory synapses. Tutoring also causes rapid inhibitory synapse insertion, but this structural imbalance is eliminated during song maturation. The work suggests that sensory exposure triggers goal-specific motor circuit development by increasing relative inhibition strength and proposes a synapse-elimination model of song memorization.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 accurately summarize the major findings of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript. The synapse-elimination model (C98) is a reasonable synthesis of the findings, though some mechanistic details remain to be established.

results.result: Sparse tutoring did not significantly alter inhibitory synapse densities at 60 dph compared to dense tutoring.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 reports a null result with appropriate statistics (p=0.2, LME model, n=4 per group). The lack of effect on inhibitory synapses contrasts with the effect on excitatory synapses, which is an important observation for understanding the specificity of tutoring paradigm effects.
